hypotheses.text: The charge lattice is sqrt 2 times the integers, and the free-boson current has contraction $(z-w)^{-2}$.
Opposite-charge vertex phases are chosen so their leading product coefficient is +1.

conclusion: On the even lattice vertex [conformal field theory](c:conformal-field-theory) space $\bigoplus_{m\in\mathbb Z}F_{m\sqrt2}$, the currents $e(z)=X(\sqrt2,z)$, $f(z)=X(-\sqrt2,z)$, and $h(z)=\sqrt2a(z)$ obey the affine sl2 [operator product expansion](c:operator-product-expansion) at level one: $h(z)h(w)\sim2/(z-w)^2$, $h(z)e(w)\sim2e(w)/(z-w)$, $h(z)f(w)\sim-2f(w)/(z-w)$, and $e(z)f(w)\sim(z-w)^{-2}+h(w)/(z-w)$.

roles.why: Integral even charge pairings give bosonic locality and the normalized central term.
This choice fixes the sl2 root-vector and Cartan conventions.

steps.slogan: Contract the Cartan current with the two root currents.
steps.detail: The Heisenberg relation gives $a(z)X(\lambda,w)\sim\lambda X(\lambda,w)/(z-w)$. Thus $h=\sqrt2a$ yields the coefficients plus 2 and minus 2 for e and f. Its self-contraction is $2/(z-w)^2$.

steps.slogan: Expand the product of the opposite root vertices.
steps.detail: The vertex contraction exponent is $\sqrt2(-\sqrt2)=-2$, so $e(z)f(w)=(z-w)^{-2}:e(z)f(w):$. Expand the normal product at z=w. Its constant is 1, and its first derivative is $\sqrt2a(w)=h(w)$, which gives the stated simple pole.

steps.slogan: Extract the affine mode commutators from these poles.
steps.detail: Contour residues give $[h_m,h_n]=2m\delta_{m,-n}$, $[h_m,e_n]=2e_{m+n}$, $[h_m,f_n]=-2f_{m+n}$, and $[e_m,f_n]=h_{m+n}+m\delta_{m,-n}$. Equal-root products have contraction exponent +2 and no pole, so their modes commute. These are precisely affine sl2 with central level 1.

statement: For Neveu-Schwarz Majorana modes $\{\psi_r,\psi_s\}=\delta_{r,-s}$, r and s half-integers, the normal-ordered quadratic stress modes obey $[L_m,L_n]=(m-n)L_{m+n}+(m^3-m)\delta_{m,-n}/24$. hypotheses.text: The modes satisfy the stated CAR, the vacuum is annihilated by positive modes, and only finite-energy vectors form the algebraic domain.

roles.why: The sums are finite on each vector and Wick contractions have the CAR signs.

steps.slogan: Derive the stress-mode action on one fermion mode.
steps.detail: The CAR gives $[L_m,\psi_r]=-(r+m/2)\psi_{m+r}$. Normal ordering makes the infinite quadratic sum locally finite. The zero-index expression is $\sum_{r>0}r\psi_{-r}\psi_r$, so the vacuum weight is zero.

steps.slogan: Reduce the commutator defect using the CAR action.
steps.detail: Jacobi with one fermion mode shows that $[L_m,L_n]-(m-n)L_{m+n}$ commutes with every CAR mode. The irreducible Fock representation makes it scalar. Energy grading forces it to vanish unless m+n=0.

steps.slogan: Compute the vacuum norm to obtain the central value.
steps.detail: For m>0 the creation-pair part of $L_{-m}\Omega$ has coefficients $(m/2-s)$ for positive half-integers s<m/2. Its norm squared is $\sum_{0<s<m/2}(m/2-s)^2=(m^3-m)/24$, with a zero coefficient at s=m/2 when present. The vacuum L_0 value is zero, so this norm is the opposite-index commutator defect.

roles.why: The strict gap makes the dyadic extension series summable and excludes point-supported ambiguity.
This condition fixes the restriction and confines any difference to the origin.

steps.slogan: Remove a shrinking neighborhood of the singular point.
steps.detail: Choose a smooth compact cutoff theta equal to 1 near zero, and define $t_n=(1-\theta(2^n x))t_0$. Each t_n is a distribution on the full space. For any exponent $\omega<\omega^{\prime}<d$, the successive annular contribution on a fixed test function is bounded by a constant times $2^{-n(d-\omega^{\prime})}$.

steps.slogan: Sum the annular terms and retain the scaling degree.
steps.detail: The geometric bound is summable, so t_n converges weakly to a continuous distribution t that extends t_0. Apply the same estimate to rescaled tests and sum from the first annulus that meets their support. The resulting bound is $|t_\lambda(f)|\leq C_f\lambda^{-\omega^{\prime}}$ for every $\omega^{\prime}>\omega$ below d, so the extension has scaling degree at most omega and its restriction gives the reverse bound.

steps.slogan: Exclude a difference supported only at the origin.
steps.detail: Two such extensions differ by a finite sum of derivatives of delta, because the difference is supported at one point. A nonzero derivative sum of highest order j has scaling degree d+j. It cannot have scaling degree below d, so the difference vanishes.

statement: For a distribution t_0 off the origin with finite scaling degree $\omega\geq d$, extensions with the same scaling degree exist. Their differences are precisely $\sum_{|\alpha|\leq\lfloor\omega-d\rfloor}c_\alpha\partial^\alpha\delta$. Thus a perturbative [quantum field theory](c:quantum-field-theory) [path integral](c:path-integral) kernel requires only finitely many local normalization constants at this point.

roles.why: Finitely many Taylor jets suffice to lower its effective singularity below d.
This condition restricts the derivative order of every local ambiguity.

steps.slogan: Subtract the test function jets through the divergence order.
steps.detail: Set $k=\lfloor\omega-d\rfloor$. Choose compact functions $w_\alpha$ with $\partial^\beta w_\alpha(0)=\delta_{\alpha\beta}$ for orders through k. The projection $Wf=f-\sum_{|\alpha|\leq k}w_\alpha\partial^\alpha f(0)$ vanishes through order k at zero, and Taylor remainder expresses it as a sum of $x^\beta f_\beta$ with $|\beta|=k+1$.

steps.slogan: Extend the remainder and assign the finite jet values.
steps.detail: Each $x^\beta t_0$ has scaling degree at most $\omega-k-1<d$, so it has a unique subcritical extension. These extensions define t on the remainder tests, and arbitrary values t(w_alpha) define it on the finite complementary jet space. The rescaled Taylor remainder estimate of Theorem 5.3 bounds both pieces by every exponent greater than omega, so the resulting extension preserves its original scaling degree. For the scaling bound, the difference between the rescaled subtraction and subtraction after rescaling is a sum of integrals $\int_\lambda^1\mu^{-d-|\alpha|-1}(t_0)_{\lambda/\mu}((x\cdot\partial-|\alpha|)w_\alpha)\,d\mu$ times the fixed jets. For every $\omega^{\prime}>\omega$, its magnitude is at most $C\lambda^{-\omega^{\prime}}\int_\lambda^1\mu^{\omega^{\prime}-d-|\alpha|-1}\,d\mu$, which is bounded because $|\alpha|\leq\omega-d$. The finite assigned delta derivatives also have scaling degree at most omega.

steps.slogan: Classify the difference between any two allowed extensions.
steps.detail: A difference supported at zero is a finite delta-derivative sum. Its highest order j has scaling degree d+j, so j must be at most k. Conversely, every such sum has scaling degree at most omega and leaves the restriction unchanged; adding it gives another allowed extension.
